title: Ten minutes of focus
hookLine: put the attention research into one sit

cards: A kitchen timer, the cheap kind that ticks, turned to ten. Ten minutes is a cup of coffee going lukewarm on the counter, the wait for a late bus. Nobody would call it long.
And yet sit with nothing but the breath for ten minutes, and the clock slows down and fills with traffic: plans, songs, arguments from last week.

Lately this path has been reading the science of attention: the gorilla people didn't see, the brain that idles, the phone on the table, the trees. Today there's no new study. All of it goes into one sit.

teach.b: First, one object. Researchers who study meditation describe two broad styles: focused attention, which rests on one thing, and open monitoring, which watches whatever comes up. Today is the first kind.

The object is the breath: always with you, always moving, so there's something to follow. Second, the drift. The resting-brain research described a mind that gets busy the moment it isn't given a job.
So expect the mind to leave the breath. That isn't the sit going wrong.
The drift is the material the sit is made of. Third, the return.
William James, in his Principles of Psychology, wrote about the power of bringing back a wandering attention "over and over again," and called it the root of judgment, character and will.
Notice what he praised: not attention that never wanders, but the bringing back. Each return is one repetition, like one lift of a weight.

Fourth, what to count. A sit where the mind wandered off again and again wasn't wasted; it was full of returns. The retreat studies this path looked at reported gains in attention, modest ones, after long practice.
So the honest promise of ten minutes isn't a calm, empty mind. It's chance after chance to notice and come back. Calm may show up some days, and some days it won't.
The returns are the training either way.

how: People who practice breath meditation may sit for a set time, such as ten minutes, resting attention on the breath and gently returning to it each time the mind wanders; teachers of this style treat each return as the practice itself.

games.q: you're a few minutes into a ten-minute sit and realize you've been planning dinner the whole time. what do you do?
o: restart the timer and try again from zero.
notice, say "back," and return to the next breath.
games.why: the return is the practice. James put the power of bringing back a wandering attention at the root of judgment, character and will.

practice: Sit upright and easy, eyes closed or resting low, and find the breath where it's clearest: the nostrils, the chest or the belly.
When you notice you've wandered off, to a plan, a tune, a worry, say one quiet word inside, "back," and return to the next breath, no scolding.
If you have the time when the bell ends, keep sitting on your own until the ten minutes are done.

wordCard.voice: Ten minutes of focus. One object, the breath, and the patient work of bringing attention back to it, again and again. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: ten minutes. Each return is one more repetition, and every one of them counts. See you tomorrow.
